briefs.area: Reconciling partial putaway against a single receipt balance
briefs.readerQuestion: How should a putaway task be recorded when only part of a received quantity has been moved to storage?
evidence: A putaway record should distinguish the quantity already placed in storage from the balance still awaiting a destination, rather than closing the receipt when the first movement is recorded.
The receiving record and the putaway task should remain linked so the same physical units are not counted as both received and still outstanding.
A parent receipt should not be marked complete while a child putaway task still shows an unplaced balance.

reviewedPlan.title: Recording Partial Putaway Without Closing the Receipt
reviewedPlan.description: How to keep a receipt open while only part of the received quantity has been moved into storage.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: A partial putaway should show placed and unplaced quantities separately, stay linked to the receipt, and not close the parent record early.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: A putaway task that has moved only part of a received quantity should record the placed quantity and the balance still awaiting a destination. The receipt should stay open and linked to that task so the same units are not counted twice. The parent receipt should not be closed while an unplaced balance remains.
operationalBasis: A putaway record should distinguish the quantity already placed in storage from the balance still awaiting a destination, rather than closing the receipt when the first movement is recorded.
The receiving record and the putaway task should remain linked so the same physical units are not counted as both received and still outstanding.
A parent receipt should not be marked complete while a child putaway task still shows an unplaced balance.
reviewedPlan.searchIntent: How should a putaway task be recorded when only part of a received quantity has been moved to storage?
outline: Separating placed quantity from the unplaced balance
Keeping the putaway task linked to its receipt
Why the parent receipt stays open
Confirming the destination balance before closing

review.rationale: Every evidence statement is a reasonable conditional deduction from the cited foundations: partial-completion supports separating placed quantity from the unplaced balance and not closing a parent record while a child task is incomplete; physical-record-alignment supports keeping the receipt and putaway task linked so the same physical units are not counted twice. The decision is distinct from published and unused briefs, which cover partial shipment permissions, unloading-sequence receipt balances, receipt-reference splits and carton-content amendments, but none address recording a partially completed putaway against a single receipt balance while keeping the parent receipt open.

briefs.area: Handling a retry of a warehouse task message already accepted
briefs.readerQuestion: How should a retried warehouse task message be checked so it does not create a second physical task for work already accepted?
evidence: A retry should preserve the identity of the original business request so the receiver can recognise work already accepted rather than treating the message as new.
Work already accepted should be distinguished from work still pending, so a retry does not silently generate another physical task.
A successful transmission should be distinguished from accepted business processing before the retry is treated as complete.

reviewedPlan.title: Checking a Retried Task Message Before It Repeats Work
reviewedPlan.description: How to confirm a retried warehouse task message does not create a duplicate physical task.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: A retry should keep the original request identity, separate accepted from pending work, and not treat transmission as acceptance.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: A retried task message should carry the identity of the original business request so already accepted work is recognised. Accepted work should be separated from work still pending before the retry is processed. Successful transmission alone should not be treated as accepted business processing.
operationalBasis: A retry should preserve the identity of the original business request so the receiver can recognise work already accepted rather than treating the message as new.
Work already accepted should be distinguished from work still pending, so a retry does not silently generate another physical task.
A successful transmission should be distinguished from accepted business processing before the retry is treated as complete.

briefs.area: Interpreting an availability statement that mixes confirmed and unconfirmed stock
briefs.readerQuestion: How should an availability statement be read when some quantities are confirmed and others are not?
evidence: An availability statement should separate known, unconfirmed, committed and physically observed quantities.
Missing confirmation should not be converted into an assumed positive availability.
A commitment should be based on the quantity basis and observation boundary stated, not on a total that mixes categories.

reviewedPlan.title: Reading Availability When Confirmed and Unconfirmed Quantities Are Mixed
reviewedPlan.description: A conditional method for separating confirmed, unconfirmed and committed quantities before acting on an availability statement.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: Split known, unconfirmed, committed and observed quantities, avoid treating missing confirmation as available, and state the observation boundary.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: An availability statement should separate known, unconfirmed, committed and physically observed quantities rather than presenting one total. Missing confirmation should not be read as available stock, and any commitment should rest on the stated quantity basis and observation boundary.
operationalBasis: An availability statement should separate known, unconfirmed, committed and physically observed quantities.
Missing confirmation should not be converted into an assumed positive availability.
A commitment should be based on the quantity basis and observation boundary stated, not on a total that mixes categories.

evidence: Client ownership and access should remain distinguishable from physical product identity and location.
Changing a contact or shared work assignment should not itself transfer stock ownership.
Where ownership is unclear, the question should be resolved before stock is treated as another client's.

Changing a contact or shared work assignment should not itself transfer stock ownership.

briefs.area: Retrying a carrier booking after an unconfirmed response
briefs.readerQuestion: When a carrier booking request times out with no confirmation, what should be checked before the same shipment is booked again?
evidence: A retried booking should carry the original shipment and booking request reference so the carrier response can be matched to the first attempt rather than treated as a new request.
A timeout or missing response should be treated as unconfirmed, not as a failed booking, until the carrier's acceptance or rejection is established.
If a second booking is confirmed, the record should distinguish the accepted booking from the earlier unconfirmed attempt so the shipment is not tendered twice.

reviewedPlan.title: Rechecking a Carrier Booking After an Unconfirmed Response
reviewedPlan.description: How to treat a timed-out carrier booking as unconfirmed and avoid tendering the same shipment twice on retry.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: A missing carrier response is not a failed booking. Preserve the original request reference and confirm acceptance before rebooking.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: A booking request without a confirmed response should be treated as unconfirmed rather than failed. The retry should carry the original request and shipment reference so any carrier acceptance can be matched to the first attempt. Only after the earlier attempt is established as not accepted should a second booking be confirmed, and the accepted booking should be distinguishable from the unconfirmed one.
operationalBasis: A retried booking should carry the original shipment and booking request reference so the carrier response can be matched to the first attempt rather than treated as a new request.
A timeout or missing response should be treated as unconfirmed, not as a failed booking, until the carrier's acceptance or rejection is established.
If a second booking is confirmed, the record should distinguish the accepted booking from the earlier unconfirmed attempt so the shipment is not tendered twice.
reviewedPlan.searchIntent: When a carrier booking request times out with no confirmation, what should be checked before the same shipment is booked again?
outline: Why a timeout is not a rejection
Keeping the original request and shipment reference on retry

Recording the accepted booking apart from the unconfirmed attempt

review.rationale: Each evidence statement follows from retry-continuity (preserve original request identity, distinguish accepted from pending, avoid a second physical task) and interface-contracts (distinguish successful transmission from accepted business processing). briefs.area: Comparing two exception reports with different scopes
briefs.readerQuestion: When two exception reports show different counts for the same warehouse issue, what should be checked before treating the difference as a real change?
evidence: Each exception report should state its observation window, included locations or statuses and the calculation basis before its count is compared with another.
A difference between reports should first be attributed to scope or definition differences rather than assumed to reflect a change in the underlying exceptions.
If the definitions cannot be made compatible, the comparison should be reported as not comparable instead of presenting a trend.

reviewedPlan.title: Comparing Exception Counts When Two Reports Disagree
reviewedPlan.description: A method for checking whether differing exception counts come from scope or definition differences before treating them as a trend.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: Two exception reports can differ because of window, scope or calculation basis. Confirm definitions match before reading a change.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: Before reading a difference between two exception reports as a real change, each report's observation window, included scope and calculation basis should be compared. A mismatch in any of these should be resolved or stated as the explanation. Where definitions cannot be aligned, the reports should be described as not comparable rather than shown as a trend.
operationalBasis: Each exception report should state its observation window, included locations or statuses and the calculation basis before its count is compared with another.
A difference between reports should first be attributed to scope or definition differences rather than assumed to reflect a change in the underlying exceptions.
If the definitions cannot be made compatible, the comparison should be reported as not comparable instead of presenting a trend.

outline: Checking observation windows first
Comparing included locations and statuses
Aligning the calculation basis
Reporting a non-comparable result honestly

review.rationale: The evidence is grounded in reporting-boundaries (state observation window, included scope, calculation basis; do not compare on matching column names alone) and exception-resolution (identify the exact information still needed). briefs.area: Reconciling a retried export against a reporting window
briefs.readerQuestion: When an incremental stock export is retried, how should the receiving report avoid counting the same transactions twice in its window?
evidence: The retried export should preserve the original batch boundary and transaction references so the receiver can recognise transactions already accepted.
The receiving report should state its observation window and exclude transactions already accepted under the earlier batch rather than summing both deliveries.
If the boundary of the retry cannot be matched to the earlier batch, the affected window should be flagged as uncertain instead of reported as a clean total.

reviewedPlan.title: Keeping a Retried Stock Export From Doubling a Report Window
reviewedPlan.description: How a receiving report should treat a retried incremental export so already accepted transactions are not counted twice.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: A retried export can repeat transactions. Match the batch boundary and exclude already accepted rows before reporting a window total.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: A retried export should keep the original batch boundary and transaction references so the receiver can identify rows already accepted. The report should exclude those accepted transactions from its window total rather than adding both deliveries. Where the retry boundary cannot be matched to the earlier batch, the window should be flagged as uncertain rather than presented as a clean total.
operationalBasis: The retried export should preserve the original batch boundary and transaction references so the receiver can recognise transactions already accepted.
The receiving report should state its observation window and exclude transactions already accepted under the earlier batch rather than summing both deliveries.
If the boundary of the retry cannot be matched to the earlier batch, the affected window should be flagged as uncertain instead of reported as a clean total.
reviewedPlan.searchIntent: When an incremental stock export is retried, how should the receiving report avoid counting the same transactions twice in its window?
outline: Why a retry can repeat transactions
Matching the retry to the original batch boundary
Excluding already accepted rows from the window
Flagging an unmatched boundary as uncertain

review.rationale: The evidence follows from retry-continuity (preserve original request identity, distinguish accepted from pending) and reporting-boundaries (state observation window and calculation basis; flag incompatible definitions).
